doc.title: Ben Sidran interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 15, 2023

title: His son pulls him back onto the road
summary: Blue Mitchell aside, then his son at sixteen urged him to play gigs in 1992 after he had been producing.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: And you got to see Blue Mitchell doing a hip little dance as he listened to a playback.

Oh my God, I love Blue Mitchell. And so my son, God bless him, he would never let me show him anything, tell him anything about music or anything. And I did not encourage him. But I love hanging out with him. He’s just a great guy. And so his whole life was spent on the road or in recording studios, and I couldn’t show him piano but he’d go up to Mac Rebennack and Mac would show him something and he’d carry on with other musicians. But never with me. He would never interact with me until later when he got to be like 16 years old. And ironically this was in 1992 I guess. And I was doing a lot of producing. I had produced Mose, I had produced Van Morrison’s record, there was a Diana Ross thing. I was really doing a lot of work. And I wasn’t doing a lot of performing. And I was thinking well maybe I’m done with performing. Maybe it’s enough. And just at that point when he was 16 he said, “Come on let’s go play gigs, man, come on, you and me, let’s go play.” And because of his enthusiasm I started booking more gigs. And he got me back out there and it was so funny because for all those years he wouldn’t interact with me at all, and then suddenly he totally turned me around and put me back on the road. So I’m eternally grateful that he did that because I’ve had more fun in the last 25 years than in the first 55. Yeah.
It’s harder to do the math the farther we go, doesn’t it?
